text: Chapter 1 closes with the practical question: how does lineage actually get captured? Three approaches, two open standards worth knowing by name, and the tradeoffs between them.

Manual documentation — someone who built or knows a pipeline writes down by hand what feeds what. Cheapest to start, works for small stable systems, but decays the moment the real pipeline changes and nobody remembers to update it. Static parsing — a tool reads the actual source code, SQL scripts, ETL job definitions, transformation configs, and derives lineage automatically, without running it. Scales better and stays closer to the truth, but dynamic logic built at runtime can defeat it.

Runtime capture instead observes what actually happens when a pipeline runs — which tables were read, which were written, in what order — and records that as lineage. It captures real executed behavior rather than an inference about intended behavior, the most trustworthy of the three in principle. But it requires instrumenting the running systems, and it only sees jobs that have actually executed at least once.

Capturing lineage is only half the problem — if every tool records it in its own proprietary format, lineage from a warehouse tool can't combine with lineage from an orchestration tool into one coherent picture. OpenLineage is an open specification for describing lineage events — runs, datasets, jobs — in a common format a shared backend can stitch into one graph. W3C PROV is an older, broader data model for provenance in general.

Manual documentation decays over time but suits small, stable, one-off systems. Static parsing reflects code as written and, once built, runs automatically. Runtime capture reflects what actually ran, but requires instrumentation. Most real organizations mix all three: automated capture for the technical, column-level detail feeding a pipeline, manual documentation filling gaps for legacy systems nothing else can reach, plus a business-lineage layer written and maintained by people.

This chapter covered what lineage is, why it matters, the business and technical split, the table and column granularity split, and now how it actually gets captured and standardized. Chapter 2 moves from concepts to practice: tracing lineage through real source systems, ETL and ELT pipelines, lakes and warehouses, semantic models, and all the way to Power BI dashboards.
